items.title: An AI agent hit Canada's national archives website 899 times this year, the government says nothing got through
items.body: Transluce, a US AI safety research group, found that automated AI agents sent 899 requests this year to a public records search service at Library and Archives Canada, digging into century old divorce records from 1905 to 1911. Thirteen of those requests carried what Transluce called attack payloads, probing for vulnerabilities in the system. Transluce alerted the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, which said in a public statement that there is no indication government systems were compromised, and that public websites routinely see requests like this as a normal part of the online environment.
items.tease: Next: why Apple just locked down what AI agents on your Mac can see.
items.reelLine: An AI agent sent 899 requests, 13 of them attack attempts, at Canada's own archives website. The government says nothing got through.

items.title: Apple is locking down what AI agents on your Mac are allowed to see, after a user said Meta's AI read his private messages
items.body: Apple is tightening macOS's full disk access permission, which can expose files, emails, messages, and browsing history once granted, after a tech columnist said Meta's Muse AI assistant referenced a private conversation he never gave it permission to read. Meta disputes his account. Apple said some developers are using full disk access in ways that put users at risk without users' full knowledge and understanding, and that AI agents have increased the risk tied to that level of access. Granting full disk access will now require explicit user action.
items.tease: Next: the AI model that just got 80% cheaper to run.
items.reelLine: Apple is locking down full disk access on Macs after a user said Meta's AI assistant read a private conversation without permission.

items.title: OpenAI cut the price of near top tier AI by 80% this week, aimed straight at coding and office work
items.body: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Sol, a model it says nearly matches the intelligence of its flagship Astra model on coding, computer use, and professional work, at one fifth of Astra's standard price: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input priced at 10 cents per million tokens. OpenAI says a typical task that costs $23 to $24 on its top models runs about $5.47 on Sol. It's available now in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the OpenAI API.
items.tease: Next: the small business program OpenAI is funding across a thousand towns like ours.
items.reelLine: OpenAI cut the price of its near top AI model by 80%, pricing a typical task at $5.47 instead of $23.

items.title: OpenAI is training 150 small business advisors to run free AI workshops, aiming to reach 1,000 small businesses
items.body: OpenAI partnered with America's SBDC, a US network serving about one million entrepreneurs a year, to train roughly 150 small business development center advisors through in person workshops, with a goal of reaching at least 1,000 small businesses. Advisors and clients who complete a workshop get free access to ChatGPT Plus. Alongside the partnership, OpenAI published a report finding that in one week in September, around 4 million employees at small firms worldwide used its tools.
items.tease: Next: the social club that cut its grant application time from three days to two hours.
items.reelLine: OpenAI is training 150 US small business advisors to run free AI workshops, aiming to reach 1,000 small businesses.

items.title: A small business cut its grant paperwork from 3 days to 2 hours using an AI tool anyone can subscribe to
items.body: The Den, a social club in Denver opening a second location, said using ChatGPT Work cut the time its leadership spends on paperwork by 10 to 15 hours a week: grant applications that used to take 3 days now take about 2 hours, and liquor license application materials dropped from 4 days to 3 hours. When an earlier hearing slot opened up, the team used the tool to pull together documents, spot what was missing, and reformat files in an afternoon instead of scrambling for days. Founder Chandler Lipe said ChatGPT Work lets the club build the company it needs before it has the size or resources of that company.

cover.hook: A Thunder Bay business can draft its next grant application in under an hour this week, using the free version of ChatGPT
cover.sub: A US social club just used the same kind of tool to cut grant application prep from 3 days to 2 hours. Here's how a Northwestern Ontario business could do the same before a FedNor, NOHFC, or NOIC deadline.

list.title: Pull your source material into one place
list.body: Before opening any AI tool, gather what a grant application actually asks for: your business registration, last year's financials, a short project description, and the program's eligibility page. ChatGPT can only work with what you give it.

list.title: Ask it to draft, not decide
list.body: Paste your project description and the program's requirements, then ask ChatGPT, the free version works for this, to draft a first pass of the application narrative in the program's own language. Treat the output as a draft to edit, not a finished answer.

list.title: Have it check your draft against the checklist
list.body: Paste the program's eligibility criteria and ask ChatGPT to flag anything your draft is missing, or any claim that isn't backed up by what you gave it. This is the step that caught gaps for The Den before its own deadline.

list.title: Reformat for whatever the program actually wants
list.body: Ask it to convert your draft into the program's required format: a specific form, a word count, a section order. Reformatting by hand is most of what eats a full day; this collapses it to minutes.

list.title: Read it yourself before anything gets submitted
list.body: Every fact, dollar figure, and date in the final draft is still your responsibility. Confirm eligibility and every number directly with the program before you submit. An AI draft is a starting point, not a source.

why.title: Why it matters
why.body: Grant season in Northwestern Ontario runs year round; FedNor, NOHFC, and NOIC all take applications continuously. The paperwork, not the eligibility, is what eats a week. The free version of a tool already on most phones can take the formatting and first draft work off that week.

cover.hook: Thunder Bay's innovation centre will help pay a local business to hire a student for an AI project this summer
cover.sub: The Northwestern Ontario Innovation Centre's Youth Tech Impact Program funds a 15 week placement, and nearly every project in its first cohort involved building or integrating AI.

posts.detailChip: Youth Tech Impact Program, Northwestern Ontario Innovation Centre
posts.title: What the program does
posts.body: The Northwestern Ontario Innovation Centre, based at Confederation College in Thunder Bay, runs the Youth Tech Impact Program. It funds a Northwestern Ontario business to hire a full time youth aged 18 to 29 for a 15 week summer placement built around a clearly defined tech or AI project, covering the youth's wage plus a completion top up. In its first cohort, the program connected nine youth with companies across the region, and most of those projects involved implementing or integrating AI into the company's own operations. The federal government announced $456,000 in new funding for the program in September, part of more than $634,000 spent on three AI related projects across Northern Ontario.

why.title: Why it matters
why.body: Most of the AI funding conversation in this region is about a business applying for money to buy a tool. This program does something different: it puts a motivated young person inside a Northwestern Ontario business for a summer specifically to build the AI project the business hasn't had time to start on its own, and the business only pays a top up for results.

cover.hook: A Thunder Bay clothing retailer selling online is now competing with a dressing room that lives inside ChatGPT
cover.sub: OpenAI's chat app can now show a shopper wearing an item before they buy it, using nothing but a selfie. For a small apparel retailer, that's a new bar for what an online product page needs to do.

posts.detailChip: ChatGPT virtual try on, what it means for apparel retail
posts.title: What changed and what it means for a local retailer
posts.body: OpenAI rolled out a Try On feature inside ChatGPT's shopping results: a shopper taps a button on a clothing or accessory listing, uploads a selfie or full body photo, and ChatGPT generates an image of them wearing the item, built on OpenAI's Images 2.5 model. A Favorites library lets shoppers save items to revisit later. OpenAI keeps the uploaded photo and can train on it unless a user opts out, worth knowing before recommending the feature to a customer.

why.title: Why it matters for local retail
why.body: A Northwestern Ontario clothing or outdoor gear retailer selling online isn't competing only with other local stores anymore; they're competing with a shopping experience that lets a customer see themselves in an item before they buy, built by a company with no storefront here at all. The practical response isn't building that feature yourself, it's making sure your own product photos, sizing information, and return policy are good enough that a shopper doesn't need to go find that experience somewhere else.

cover.hook: There's a federal program built specifically to help a Northern Ontario business adopt AI, and it covers up to 75% of what isn't hardware
cover.sub: FedNor's Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative funds AI commercialization and adoption projects across Northern Ontario. Confirm eligibility and current funding availability with FedNor before applying.

posts.title: Who it's for and how it works
posts.body: RAII is a continuous intake FedNor program that supports AI commercialization and adoption in Northern Ontario: helping AI scale ups bring a product to market, and helping other small and medium businesses integrate AI into their own operations. It covers up to 50% of capital costs and up to 75% of non capital costs for for profit applicants. It's open to incorporated SMEs, not for profits, Indigenous communities and organizations, and municipalities across Northern Ontario, though retail and service based businesses are excluded. The application runs through a two phase FedNor portal process, and FedNor asks applicants to contact an officer before applying.

why.title: Why it matters
why.body: This is one of the only funding programs built around AI specifically rather than technology adoption broadly, which matters for a Northwestern Ontario business trying to fund an AI project rather than a general equipment upgrade. The exclusion of retail and service businesses is real, so confirm your business type qualifies with FedNor before building a proposal around it.

cover.hook: The gap between what Silicon Valley can run and what a Northwestern Ontario business can afford just got a lot smaller
cover.sub: This week alone: OpenAI's near top model got 80% cheaper, its fastest model got up to 8 times faster on new NVIDIA chips, and NVIDIA released a $4,999 box that runs a serious AI model with no cloud bill at all.

posts.title: The real story this week isn't a new model, it's the price of the old one
posts.body: Three things happened to AI's cost and speed in the same week. OpenAI cut the price of a near top tier model, GPT-6.1 Sol, to a fifth of its flagship's price, running a typical task for about $5.47 instead of $23. NVIDIA said its newest Blackwell chips make OpenAI's fastest model, GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast, generate answers up to 8 times faster than its standard tier. And NVIDIA launched a $4,999 desktop box, the DGX Spark 64GB, built to run AI models up to 100 billion parameters locally, no cloud subscription required. None of these is a smarter model. All three are the same capability becoming cheaper, faster, and more ownable than it was a month ago.

why.title: Why it matters here
why.body: A Northwestern Ontario business doesn't need San Francisco money to use the AI a San Francisco company is using this month, it needs to notice that the price and the hardware both just moved in its direction. The businesses that benefit from a price collapse like this one are rarely the ones that built the technology. They're whoever in a place like Thunder Bay decides to actually put it to use first, while everywhere else is still catching up to the new price.
